intro:
These exercises move ownership, borrowing, and lifetimes out of syntax and into design. The order the chapter insists on holds throughout: decide who owns a value first, decide who may temporarily borrow it second, and only then reach for an explicit lifetime when the compiler genuinely needs you to relate one borrow to another. Most real borrow-checker friction is not a rule you broke; it is an ownership decision you have not made yet.

The through-line is a service boundary. Request bytes arrive borrowed, get inspected and normalized while they stay local, and become owned the moment they cross into something that must outlive the request: a queue, a cache, a stored record, an async task. The warm-up trains you to narrate that flow, the implementation and refactoring exercises make you produce it in code, and the design exercise asks you to commit to concrete owners at every subsystem edge. Each solution names the owner, the borrow, and the boundary, because that triple is what the rest of the book builds on.

exerciseSolutions.title: Tell the ownership story before touching syntax
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Walk the four stages and name an owner or a borrower at each one. The original request bytes are owned by whoever received them from the socket: the ingress layer holds the buffer (a Vec<u8> or an equivalent owned region). Everything downstream that only reads those bytes should borrow them as &[u8] rather than take a copy, because no downstream stage needs an independent buffer while it is merely inspecting.

Header validation borrows. It receives &[u8], scans for the fields it needs, and returns a yes/no or a small set of parsed offsets. It never needs to retain the buffer past its own call, so it should take a temporary shared borrow and nothing more. Building the routing key is the transition point. While the key is being derived it can borrow slices of the request buffer, but the key that comes out is a derived, normalized value, and the moment it is going to live past the request it must become owned: a String, or a small owned struct, not a &str pointing back into the buffer.

The worker queue is the boundary that forces ownership. A job placed on a queue can be picked up by another thread, can sit there after the request handler returns, and can outlive the request buffer entirely. A reference into the request buffer would be a dangling promise: the buffer's owner (the ingress layer) may drop it as soon as the handler returns, which is before the worker ever runs. So the queue must receive owned data. This is the chapter's core operational rule made concrete: borrow while local, transfer ownership when the next stage can outlive the current scope.
criteria: Names an owner for the request bytes: the ingress layer that received them from the socket holds the owned buffer.
Separates borrowed inspection (header validation, key derivation read slices via &[u8]) from owned cross-boundary data (the job sent to the queue).
Explains the queue boundary as an ownership transfer point because the job can outlive and run after the request buffer's owner drops it.

exerciseSolutions.title: Find the unnecessary clone
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The helper clones path into path_copy, prints path_copy, then keeps using the original path. Ask the operational question the chapter trains: does any code need an independent, separately-owned copy of the path? Here it does not. Printing only reads the string, and the original path is still valid and still used right after. The clone produces a second owned String that is read once and dropped, which is pure allocation and copy cost with no semantic purpose. It is a borrow-checker reflex, not a duplication the design requires.

The first repair is to borrow. Printing needs read access, and read access is exactly what a shared borrow grants. Pass &path (or just print path directly, since println! borrows its arguments), and delete path_copy entirely. Nothing about the program's meaning changes, and you save an allocation on every call. If the helper's job were instead to produce a value that must outlive the original buffer, the right move would be to return ownership from the helper, not to clone internally and discard, so that the caller decides the lifetime of the result.

A clone is justified when you genuinely need a second value with an independent lifetime: when you must mutate one copy while preserving the original, when an owned value has to be stored or sent somewhere that outlives the source, or when an API you cannot change demands an owned String. None of those apply to a read-and-print. The discipline is not 'never clone'; it is 'clone only when independent ownership is the point, and say why.'
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Replacing a read-only clone with a shared borrow removes an allocation without changing meaning.
criteria: Distinguishes semantic duplication (a real second owner with its own lifetime) from a borrow-checker work-around (this clone, read once and dropped).
Proposes borrowing first: the path is only read, so &str / a shared borrow is sufficient and the clone is deleted.
Justifies a remaining clone only when independent ownership is required (mutate-while-preserving, store/send past the source, or an owned-only API).

exerciseSolutions.title: Accept borrowed input and return owned output
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The signature is the whole point: fn build_cache_key(service: &str, route: &str) -> String. The two inputs are borrowed because the function only reads them to assemble the key; it has no reason to take ownership of the caller's strings. The output is owned (String) because a cache key is exactly the kind of value that outlives the inputs: it gets inserted into a map, hashed, retained across calls. Returning &str here would be wrong because there is nothing for it to borrow from that outlives the call, the key is newly constructed, so it must be owned.

Use format! to build the result in one allocation: format!("{}:{}", service, route). This reads both borrowed inputs and produces a single owned String. There are no intermediate clones, the only allocation is the final result itself, which is unavoidable because the caller asked for an owned value. The colon separator gives billing:/v1/invoices and search:/ready for the sample inputs.

This is the chapter's strong default for service code in miniature: borrow for inspection and assembly, return owned when the result must be decoupled from the input buffers' lifetimes. The caller can drop service and route immediately after the call and the returned key remains valid, which is precisely the independence a cache key needs.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Borrowed &str inputs, a single owned String result built with one allocation.
criteria: Signature is exactly fn build_cache_key(service: &str, route: &str) -> String.
Output matches billing:/v1/invoices and search:/ready for the sample inputs.
Returns owned data: format! builds a new String, so the result does not borrow from the inputs or any temporary.

exerciseSolutions.title: Annotate lifetimes only where required
exerciseSolutions.solution:
first_word(s: &str) -> &str has exactly one input borrow, and the returned slice can only come from that one input. There is no ambiguity for the compiler to resolve, so lifetime elision applies: Rust reads the single input lifetime as the output lifetime automatically. The signature stays as written. Adding an explicit lifetime, fn first_word<'a>(s: &'a str) -> &'a str, is legal but changes nothing about the model; it documents a relationship that was never in doubt and just adds noise.

pick_longer is different because it returns one of two input borrows. The compiler cannot guess whether the output borrows from left or from right, and the answer is 'it could be either depending on the runtime comparison.' That forces you to name the relationship: fn pick_longer<'a>(left: &'a str, right: &'a str) -> &'a str. Tying both inputs and the output to the same lifetime 'a tells the compiler the returned reference is valid only as long as both inputs are valid, which is the only sound contract for a function that might return either one.

The key conceptual point, and the reason this exercise pairs the two functions, is what the annotation does and does not do. The 'a on pick_longer does not extend how long anything is stored; the underlying strings live exactly as long as they were going to. It documents a constraint: the caller may use the result only within the overlap of the two inputs' lifetimes. Annotation describes a borrowing relationship the compiler must verify; it never grants extra storage. That is why adding 'a to first_word is harmless but pointless, while leaving it off pick_longer is a compile error.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Elision where one input borrow exists; one shared lifetime where the output may come from either input.
criteria: Keeps fn first_word(s: &str) -> &str elided, since the single input borrow makes the output relationship unambiguous.
Annotates pick_longer with one lifetime 'a tying both inputs and the output together, the only sound contract when either input may be returned.
Explains the annotation documents a borrowing relationship the compiler must verify, and never extends how long any value is stored.

exerciseSolutions.title: Fix a borrow-checker failure without cloning
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Name the conflict precisely first, because the chapter is explicit that this is not a rule violation in the abstract. first holds a shared borrow into buffer (first_word(&buffer) returns a &str slice of buffer). buffer.clear() needs a mutable borrow of buffer. Then first is printed, which means the shared borrow must still be live at the clear(). The shared borrow and the exclusive borrow overlap in time, and overlapping shared-plus-exclusive borrows of the same value are the one forbidden state. The defect is borrow duration, not the borrowing rules being wrong.

The cleanest repair is to shorten the shared borrow so it ends before the mutation begins. Move the use of first ahead of buffer.clear(): print first while the borrow is still valid, and only then clear the buffer. Once the println! is done, the slice is no longer used, the borrow ends (non-lexical lifetimes end a borrow at its last use), and clear() is free to take its exclusive borrow. No clone, no allocation, just sequencing: inspect first, mutate second.

Reach for owned data only if the later code genuinely needs the word after the buffer is mutated, for example if you must print first after clear(). Then converting to an owned value, let first = first_word(&buffer).to_string();, is the justified move, because you really do need a value with a lifetime independent of buffer. The justification is concrete (the value must survive the mutation), not a reflex to silence the compiler. Wrapping the borrow in an inner scope is a third option that makes the duration visually obvious, but here simple reordering is enough.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Reordering ends the shared borrow before the mutation; owning is reserved for when the value must outlive the mutation.
criteria: Repair ends the shared borrow before the mutable clear() by moving the use of first earlier (or converts to owned only for a stated reason).
Does not default to cloning; the to_string() path is presented only when the word must survive the mutation, with that need named.
Explains the conflict as overlapping borrow duration (shared and exclusive borrows live at the same time), not as a borrowing rule being violated in principle.

exerciseSolutions.title: Choose ownership for a long-lived service API
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Map owners and borrowers onto the flow socket bytes -> parse route -> normalize key -> store record -> publish async notification, and the line between borrowed and owned falls in a predictable place. The socket bytes are owned by the ingress layer that read them into a buffer. parse_route and normalize_key both accept borrowed input: parse_route(bytes: &[u8]) inspects the buffer and returns the parsed pieces, and normalize_key(raw: &str) -> String reads the parsed route and produces a canonical key. These stages are local, they finish before the request handler returns, and they have no reason to take ownership of the buffer.

Ownership has to appear before storage and before the async notification. The stored record must be an owned struct, AuditRecord { service: String, key: String, received_at: Instant }, with owned fields, because it lives in a database, a write buffer, or an in-memory store long after the request buffer is gone. The async notification is even stricter: a spawned task may run on another thread and after the handler returns, so the notification payload must be 'static-friendly owned data (an owned struct or String), never a reference into the request buffer. Both boundaries are ownership-transfer points for the same reason as the queue in Exercise 1: the next stage can outlive the current owner.

A borrowed-field struct, struct ParsedRoute<'a> { method: &'a str, path: &'a str }, is justified only as a short-lived view used inside parsing and normalization, where it never escapes the scope that owns the buffer. It is the wrong default for the stored record or the notification, because a lifetime parameter on a long-lived struct couples that struct to the request buffer's lifetime and forces the buffer to stay alive for as long as the record does, which defeats the point of storing it. The tradeoff I am accepting is explicit: converting to owned data at the storage and async edges costs allocations (each record and notification allocates its Strings), in exchange for decoupled lifetimes, a simpler API where stored and queued types are plain owned structs with no lifetime parameters, and long-term maintainability, because adding a new consumer of the record never has to reason about the request buffer. For an audit service, where records are durable and notifications are fire-and-forget, that allocation cost is the right thing to pay; the borrowed view stays confined to the hot, local parsing path where it actually saves work.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Borrowed view for local parsing; owned structs at the storage and async edges, with no lifetime parameter escaping into long-lived types.
criteria: Keeps borrowed input local: parse_route and normalize_key take borrows, and the borrowed ParsedRoute view never escapes parsing/normalization.
Converts to owned form before storage and async: AuditRecord holds Strings and the notification payload is an owned String.
Justifies a tradeoff explicitly: paying per-record/notification allocations to get decoupled lifetimes, a simpler lifetime-free API, and maintainability.
Does not present borrowed fields in long-lived structs as the default; the borrowed-field struct is scoped to parsing only, with the lifetime-coupling cost named.

labSolution.explanation:
The initial code returns route.to_string(), which drops the service entirely and prints only the route. The fix builds the full key from both borrowed inputs: format!("{}:{}", service, route) reads service and route and produces one owned String in a single allocation, with no intermediate clones.

The two inputs stay borrowed as &str because the function only reads them to assemble the key, while the result is owned because a cache key is meant to outlive the inputs: it gets inserted into a map, hashed, or retained across calls. This is the chapter's strong default in one line, borrow for inspection, return owned when the result must be decoupled from the caller's buffers.

main calls the function twice. The first call joins billing and /v1/invoices with a colon to print billing:/v1/invoices; the second joins search and /ready to print search:/ready. Each println! adds its own newline, producing the two expected lines exactly.

reviewAnswers.question: Why is ownership usually the first question and lifetimes the second?
reviewAnswers.answer: Ownership decides who is responsible for a value, who cleans it up, and whether the next stage merely observes the data or must outlive the current owner. Once that is settled, a lifetime is just the compiler's name for how long a particular borrow stays valid, a detail that only arises after you have already decided to borrow rather than transfer ownership. Asking lifetimes first inverts the model and leads to the common mistake of adding lifetime annotations to paper over what is really an ownership decision. Decide the owner, then borrow, then annotate only if the compiler needs the relationship spelled out.

reviewAnswers.question: What is the operational difference between `&T` and `&mut T`?
reviewAnswers.answer: &T is a shared borrow: it grants read-only access, and many &T borrows of the same value may exist at once because no one is mutating through them. &mut T is an exclusive borrow: it grants the ability to mutate, and Rust permits only one at a time with no other borrows alive, because aliasing plus mutation is where memory and concurrency bugs are born. Operationally you reach for &T when the callee only inspects data and &mut T when it must change the value. The borrow checker enforces that a value is, at any moment, either freely shared among readers or held by exactly one writer, never both.

reviewAnswers.question: What does a lifetime annotation describe, and what does it never do?
reviewAnswers.answer: A lifetime annotation describes a relationship between borrows, most often which input a returned reference borrows from, so the compiler can verify the output is never used past the validity of that input. It is a constraint you are documenting for the compiler to check, not a runtime mechanism. It never extends how long a value is stored or keeps anything alive; the underlying data lives exactly as long as it would without the annotation. That is why adding a lifetime to a single-input function changes nothing, while a function returning one of two inputs needs the annotation to state which borrowing relationship must hold.

reviewAnswers.question: When is returning `String` cleaner than returning `&str`?
reviewAnswers.answer: Returning String is cleaner whenever the result must outlive or be decoupled from the inputs, when it is newly constructed, normalized, or formatted and there is nothing borrowable that lives long enough to back a &str. A cache key, an audit label, or any value built with format! falls into this category: it has no source to borrow from, so it must own its data. Returning &str only makes sense when the output is a slice of an input that the caller keeps alive, like the first word of a borrowed string. If the result is going to be stored, queued, retried, or returned across a boundary, String frees the caller from the input's lifetime and is the right choice.

reviewAnswers.question: Why do queue, cache, and async boundaries often push you toward owned data?
reviewAnswers.answer: Each of these boundaries lets a value live past the scope that produced it: a queued job runs later, possibly on another thread; a cache entry is retained across calls; an async task may execute after the spawning function returns. A reference into a local buffer would dangle the moment that buffer's owner drops it, which typically happens before the next stage runs. So the next stage must receive owned data with an independent lifetime, making these boundaries natural ownership-transfer points. This is the same rule everywhere: if a later stage can outlive the current scope, it should own its data rather than borrow from that scope.
